name: Sysmon (System Monitor)
os_min: Windows 7 / Server 2008 R2 and later (Sysmon is a Sysinternals tool, not a default Windows component, and must be separately installed and configured)
purpose: A Microsoft Sysinternals kernel-mode driver and service that logs detailed system activity - process creation with full command lines, network connections, file creation, registry changes, and more - to the Windows event log, extremely rarely present by default but very commonly deployed for DFIR and detection engineering.
key_fields: Event ID 1 - Process Create: full command line, hashes (SHA1 default, or MD5/SHA256/IMPHASH), ProcessGuid, parent process info
Event ID 3 - Network Connection: source process, source/destination IP and port, hostnames (disabled by default)
Event ID 7 - Image Loaded: DLL/module load into a process, with hash and signature info (disabled by default, high volume)
Event ID 8 - CreateRemoteThread: source and target process, thread start address/module/function - a common process injection indicator
Event ID 10 - ProcessAccess: one process opening a handle to another (e.g., access to lsass.exe for credential theft)
Event ID 11 - FileCreate: a file was created or overwritten, useful for monitoring autostart and staging locations
Event ID 12/13/14 - RegistryEvent: key/value create-delete, value set, and key/value rename respectively
Event ID 22 - DNSEvent: a process performed a DNS query (Windows 8.1+ only)
ProcessGuid / LogonGuid - unique correlation identifiers that survive PID reuse, used to stitch related events together
normal_baseline: Event volume and content dependent entirely on the deployed Sysmon configuration file; on a well-tuned config, Event ID 1 (process creation) reflects known software launching from expected paths with plausible parent-child relationships, and configured network/file/registry events match approved application behavior.
anomalies: Event ID 1 process creation with a suspicious parent-child relationship (e.g., an Office application spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe) or a command line containing encoded/obfuscated content
Event ID 8 (CreateRemoteThread) targeting a sensitive process such as lsass.exe or a browser process, indicating likely code injection
Event ID 10 (ProcessAccess) showing a non-standard process opening a handle to lsass.exe with access rights consistent with memory-reading tools (a classic credential-dumping indicator)
Event ID 1 showing process creation events abruptly stop while other logs (Security, System) continue - possible Sysmon tampering or filter-rule abuse rather than expected quiet
Event ID 11 (FileCreate) writing an executable into an unusual autostart location (Startup folder, Run key target directory) shortly before a corresponding Event ID 1 executing it
Registry events (12/13/14) creating or modifying known persistence keys (e.g., Run/RunOnce) from an unexpected parent process
anti_forensic_notes: Sysmon explicitly does not attempt to hide itself or its driver from attackers, and its own documentation notes it provides no self-protection beyond running as a protected process; an attacker with sufficient privileges can uninstall it (sysmon -u), stop its service, or tamper with the 'Start'/'Enable' values under its EventLog-Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon-Operational Autologger registry key to silently suppress future logging without necessarily generating an obvious Sysmon-specific alert. Because Sysmon coverage and event volume depend entirely on the deployed configuration file, a gap in expected event types (e.g., no Event ID 3 network connections at all) may simply mean that event type was never enabled, not that it was tampered with - the configuration in place must be checked before drawing conclusions from absence.
